opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the basic issue is that if you want to use a language model as a model of how humans learn language, rather than just as an engineering artifact, then the conditions under which the model learns have to bear some resemblance to the conditions under which a child learns. And the most glaring mismatch right now is the amount of data. A child is exposed to something on the order of tens of millions of words by the time they're, say, ten or twelve years old, maybe a hundred million if you're being generous. The large models people are excited about are trained on hundreds of billions or trillions of words. That's several orders of magnitude more than any human will ever hear or read in their lifetime.

Why does that matter? Because a lot of the questions we care about in cognitive science are questions about what you can learn from the input that's actually available to you. The classic debate, the poverty of the stimulus argument, is precisely about whether the data children get is rich enough to support learning, say, the hierarchical structure of syntax, or whether you need some innate bias toward that kind of structure. If a model succeeds after seeing a thousand times more data than a child, that doesn't tell you much about that question. Maybe the model needed all that extra data to compensate for lacking the right inductive biases. Success in that regime is compatible with both sides of the argument.

So when you restrict the model to a developmentally plausible amount of data, the results become much more informative. If a model with fairly generic architecture learns, say, subject-verb agreement across intervening clauses, or the right generalization for question formation, from a child-sized corpus, that's evidence that those generalizations are learnable without very specific built-in knowledge. And if it fails, and in a lot of our work we've found that models at that scale do make non-humanlike generalizations, that's also informative. It points to the kinds of biases you might need to add, and then you can actually test hypotheses about what those biases are.

There's also a practical, almost methodological benefit. Models trained on small data are cheap enough that academic labs can train many of them, vary the architecture, vary the training data, and run controlled experiments, which is what you want if you're doing science rather than just evaluating one giant pretrained system you didn't build and whose training data you can't inspect.

And I'd add one caveat, which is that matching the number of words isn't the whole story. Children aren't just passively reading text; they're interacting with people, they have a visual world, they have communicative goals. So a text-only model trained on a hundred million words is still a pretty impoverished learner in some ways, and richer in others. But data quantity is the first-order mismatch, and you have to address it before the comparison to humans even starts to make sense.

r001.rationale: The response says a model intended to represent human language learning should learn under conditions resembling a child’s, and that limiting data to a developmentally plausible amount makes comparisons with humans more informative.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is: if we want to use a language model as a model of how humans learn and process language, the model has to face a problem that's at least roughly comparable to the one a human child faces. And the data regime is a huge part of that.

A child hears something on the order of tens of millions of words by the time they're five or so, maybe up to a hundred million by early adolescence depending on how you count. Models like GPT-3 and its successors are trained on hundreds of billions, or trillions, of words. That's three or four orders of magnitude more linguistic input than any human ever gets in a lifetime. So when a model like that does something impressively human-like, say it handles subject-verb agreement across an intervening clause, or it generalizes some syntactic constraint to a novel case, it's hard to know what to make of that for cognitive science. Maybe it learned the generalization in a human-like way. Or maybe it just memorized enough near-duplicates that the hard cases aren't actually hard anymore. With that much data, you can't easily tell the difference.

The question that got a lot of us into this field in the first place is a question about learning. It's the classic debate: how much of linguistic structure has to be built in, and how much can be acquired from exposure? Chomsky's argument about the poverty of the stimulus is fundamentally a claim about what can be learned from a certain amount and kind of data. If you want to use neural networks to weigh in on that debate, which I think is one of the most exciting things we could do with them, then you have to train them on something like the stimulus a child actually gets. Otherwise you're answering a different question. You're showing what's learnable in principle from unlimited data, which is interesting, but it's not the question developmental linguists care about.

There's a second reason that's a bit more practical. When models are trained on human-scale data, their failures become informative. If a model trained on a hundred million words fails to learn, say, filler-gap dependencies or some island constraint, that tells you something. Either the input doesn't carry enough signal for that generalization, which would support some kind of inductive bias story, or the architecture is missing something. Both outcomes are scientifically useful. Whereas a model trained on the whole internet almost never fails on these benchmarks anymore, and when it succeeds you've learned very little about mechanism.

And then I'd add a third thing, which is that this constraint pushes us toward asking what inductive biases actually matter. If you can't just throw more data at the problem, you have to think about what architectures or training objectives or curricula get you human-like generalization from limited input. That's a much more productive research program for cognitive science than scaling. It's also, I'd note, something that efforts like the BabyLM challenge have tried to make a community around, specifically to get people competing on sample efficiency rather than on raw scale.

So I'd put it this way. The data regime isn't a nuisance parameter you can fix later. It's the thing that determines whether the model is addressing the cognitive question at all.

r001.rationale: The response says a model of human language learning and processing must face a data regime roughly comparable to a child’s, and argues that human-scale training makes its behavior more informative for cognitive science.

astra-6.text:
Well, if we want to use language models to understand how humans learn language, then the amount of data they learn from is part of what we need to explain. A model might do very well after seeing vastly more language than a child does, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us how the child gets there with much less experience.

That doesn’t mean the model isn’t useful. It might still tell us something about what can be learned from linguistic input. But the stronger cognitive question is whether a model can acquire the relevant abilities from something closer to the input available to a child. If it can’t, we need to ask what’s missing: perhaps a different learning mechanism, some useful prior structure, or the grounding and social interaction that children have.

So learning from less data is a way of making the test more informative. We’re asking not just whether a system can learn language, but whether it can learn it under constraints that resemble ours.

r001.rationale: The response says child-like data constraints make the cognitive test more informative and asks whether models can acquire relevant abilities under them. It does not predict that doing so will make models better at modeling human language processing.

sol-6.1.text:
If we want to use language models as models of human language learning, we need to take seriously the amount of data that humans actually get. A model might do very well on some linguistic task after seeing billions or trillions of words, but that doesn’t necessarily explain how a child learns to do the same thing with much less experience.

So learning from less data is a way of making the comparison more meaningful. We can ask: given something closer to the input available to a child, what does the model learn, and where does it struggle? That can help us identify what kinds of learning mechanisms or prior assumptions might be needed to explain human language acquisition. Of course, children also have social interaction and perceptual experience, so matching the number of words alone isn’t enough. But it’s an important constraint.

r001.rationale: The response says human-like data limits make comparisons more meaningful and may help identify learning mechanisms, but it does not predict that such constraints will make language models better models of human language processing.
